IX.|TO THE ROMANES.|405}}</noinclude>Because not of faith, but as it vvere of vvorkes. for c {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ Here we see that they are the cause of their owne damnation by infidelity.}}∷ they haue stombled at the stone of stombling, {{verse|chapter=9|verse=33}}† as it is vvritten, {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Es. 8, 14. 28, 16.''}}* ''Behold I put in Sion a stone of'' stombling, and a rocke of scandal: and vvhosoeuer ''beleeueth in him, shal not be confounded''.

{{c|{{larger|A N N O T A T I O N S}}}}
{{c|{{sc|Chap. IX.}}}}

''3. Anathema.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Anathema.}}''Anáthema'', by vse of Scripture is either that vvhich by separation from profane vse, and by dedication to God, is holy, dreadful, and not vulgarly to be touched: or contrarievvise, that which is reiected, seuered, or abandoned from God, as cursed and detested, and therfore is to be auoided. And in this later sense (according as S. Paul taketh it 1 Cor. 16. ''If any loue not our Lord {{sc|Iesvs Christ}}, be he Anathema'', that is to say, Away vvith him, Accursed be he, Beware you company not vvith him) the Church and holy Councels vse the vvord for a curse and excommunication against Heretikes and other notorious offenders and blasphemers. {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=In what sense S. Paul wisheth to be anathema.}}Novv how the Apostle, vvishing him self to be Anathema from Christ to saue his Countrie mens soules, did take this vvord, it is a very hard thing to determine. Some thinke, he desired onely to die for their saluation. Others, that being very loth to be kept from the fruition of Christ, yet he could be content to be so still for to saue their soules. Others, that he vvished vvhat malediction or separation from Christ so euer that did not imply the disfauour of God tovvards him, nor take avvay his loue toward God. This only is certaine that it is a point of vnspeakable charitie in the Apostles breast, and a paterne to al Bishops and Priests, hovv to loue the saluation of their flocke. As the like vvas vttered by Moyses vvhen he said, {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Exo. 32, 32''.}}''Either forgiue this people, or blot me out of thy booke''.

''6. Not al of Israel.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Gods promis not made to carnal Israel.}}Though the people of the Ievves vvere many waies honoured and priuiledged, and namely by Christes taking flesh of them: yet the promis of grace and saluation was neither onely made to them, nor to al them that carnally came of them or their fathers: Gods election and mercie depending vpon his owne purpose, vvil, and determination, and not tied to any nation, familie, or person.

''7. But in Isaac.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Isaac preferred before Ismael.}}The promisse made to Abraham was not in Ismael, vvho vvas a sonne borne onely by flesh and nature: but in Isaac, vvho vvas a sonne obtained by promisse, faith, and miracle: and vvas a figure of the Churches children borne to God in Baptisme.

''10. Of one copulation.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Iacob before Esau.}}It is proued also by Gods choosing of Iacob before Esau (who vvere not onely brethren by father and mother, but also tvvinnes, and Esau the elder of the two, vvhich according to carnal count should haue had the preeminence) that God in giuing graces folovveth not the temporal or carnal prerogatiues of men or families.

''11. Not yet borne.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=By the example of Iacob and Esau, is shewed Gods mere mercie in the elect, and iustice in the reprobate.}}By the same example of those twinnes, it is euident also, that neither nations nor particular persons be elected eternally, or called temporally, or preferred to Gods fauour before others, by their ovvne merites: because God, vvhen he made choise, and first loued Iacob, and refused Esau, respected them both as il, and the one no lesse then the other guilty of damnation for original sinne, vvhich vvas alike in them both. And therfore vvhere iustly he might haue reprobated both, he saued of mercie one. Which one therfore, being as il and as void of good as the other, must hold of Gods eternal purpose, mercie, and election, that he was preferred before his brother vvhich was elder then him self, and no worse them him self. And his brother Esau on the other side hath no cause to complaine, for that God neither did nor suffered any thing to be done towards him, that his sinne did not deserue, for although God elect eternally & giue his first grace without al merites, yet he doth not reprobate or hate any man but for sinne, or the foresight thereof.

''14. Is there iniquitie.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Predestination and reprobation take not away free wil, neither must any man be retchlesse & desperate.}}Vpon the former discourse that of tvvo persons equal, God calleth the one to mercie, and leaueth the other in his sinne, one might inferre that God were vniust and an accepter of persons. To vvhich the Apostle ansvvereth, that God vvere not iust nor indifferent in deede, so to vse the matter where grace or saluation vvere due. As if two men being Christened, both beleeue wel, & liue vvel: if God should giue heauen to the one, & should damne the other, then were he vniust, partial, & forgetful of his promisse: but respecting or taking two, who both be vvorthy of damnation (as al are before they be first called to mercie) then the matter standeth on mere mercie, and of the giuers wil and liberalitie, in which case partialitie hath no place. As for example. <col-left>1 Two malefactors being condemned both for one crime, the Prince pardoneth the one, and letteth the law procede on the other. 2 The theefe that is pardoned, can not attribute his escape to his owne deseruings, but<noinclude>{{rh||Eee iij|to}}</noinclude>
